meta.title: Check your understanding: The smart grid

objectives: Explain how inertia slows the fall in frequency after a power station trips
Calculate the rate of change of frequency (RoCoF) with the swing equation
Explain the duck curve and the tools a smart grid uses to balance it

questions.prompt: As inverter-connected solar and wind replace coal and gas plants, why does the frequency fall faster after a power station trips?
choices: Inverters draw extra power from the grid whenever the frequency drops
There is less spinning mass whose stored energy can cover the shortfall
Solar and wind run at 60 Hz while the rest of the grid runs at 50 Hz
Operators lower the grid's nominal frequency to make room for renewables
questions.explain: In the first instant after a trip, the missing energy comes from spinning turbines and generators, which slow down; that spinning mass is the grid's inertia. Solar panels and most wind turbines connect through inverters with no spinning mass coupled to the grid, so as they replace fuel-burning plants the frequency falls faster.

questions.prompt: A 60 Hz grid with 30,000 MVA of spinning machines and an inertia constant H of 3 s suddenly loses 900 MW. What is the initial rate of change of frequency (RoCoF)?
questions.explain: df/dt = 900 × 60 ÷ (2 × 3 × 30,000) = 0.3 Hz/s, falling. Leaving out the factor of 2 gives 0.6 Hz/s, and 0.25 Hz/s uses 50 Hz instead of this grid's 60 Hz.

questions.prompt: On the duck curve, what makes the "belly" sag in the middle of a spring day?
choices: People use much less electricity at midday than at night
Power stations are taken offline at midday for maintenance
The curve is demand minus solar and wind, and midday solar output is large
Wind farms produce most of their power around midday
questions.explain: The duck is a plot of net load: the demand other sources must still supply after wind and solar. Demand itself does not collapse at midday; solar output is subtracted from it, and as solar grows the belly deepens while the evening peak stays.

questions.prompt: A grid has very little inertia (H = 1 s). In the trip widget, which change does most to stop the frequency dipping deep after a power station trips?
choices: Reserves, such as batteries, that take over within about a second
Larger reserves that take about 20 seconds to respond
More solar farms, to make up the lost energy over the day
Raising the grid's nominal frequency from 50 to 60 Hz
questions.explain: Speed can stand in for inertia: with H = 1 s, reserves that take over within a second hold the dip to about 49.8 Hz, while reserves that need 20 seconds let it fall to about 49.2 Hz. Batteries can respond in about a second, which is why low-inertia grids buy fast frequency response from them.
